findings.issue_text: [BUG] The 'advanced features' negative-offset path passes a negative start to Django queryset slicing, which raises ValueError('Negative indexing is not supported.') Django ORM slices do not 'handle boundary conditions automatically' as the comment claims; a cursor carrying a negative offset with enable_advanced_features=True raises a 500 on every request, contradicting the docstring's promise of negative offset support — the feature's only distinct behavior is the one that crashes.

[BUG] The prev-cursor boundary handling compares len(results) against offset + limit + extra computed from the raw negative offset, mismatching the actual slice bounds start_offset + limit + extra. For a negative offset prev cursor, the elif branch never fires when it should (or fires when it shouldn't), so the duplicated boundary row is returned to the client, producing a duplicated audit-log row in the response.

[BUG] The unconditional change to BasePaginator.get_result alters behavior for every existing paginator: when cursor.is_prev is true the offset is no longer clamped, allowing negative start_offset in the shared slice. Any existing endpoint paginating backwards with a crafted negative cursor offset now produces queryset[-N:...] which raises ValueError, turning a previously-clamped request into a 500 across all DateTimePaginator/OrganizationPaginator-style endpoints.

[ADVISORY] The new optimized_pagination behavior is gated on a raw query-string parameter with no settings flag or options entry, and it is the only gating flag on this path — but the sibling flag enable_advanced_features passed to paginate() is never validated to be an accepted kwarg of the paginate() signature. If Endpoint.paginate() does not forward unknown kwargs to the paginator constructor, the superuser path raises TypeError on every optimized request; operators also cannot disable the feature without a code deploy.

[ADVISORY] The new OptimizedCursorPaginator class (~95 lines of behavior-bearing pagination logic, including the modified shared get_result in BasePaginator) ships with no tests anywhere in the diff — no spec/test files appear, so cursor round-tripping, prev/next boundary de-duplication, and negative-offset behavior are entirely unverified. A regression in cursor construction (e.g. build_cursor consuming the mutated results list after the is_prev reverse) silently corrupts pagination for superusers browsing audit logs; nothing in the diff would catch it.

[ADVISORY] There is no verification that OptimizedCursorPaginator returns the same rows/cursors as DateTimePaginator for the same queryset — the acceptance criterion 'backward compatibility with existing cursor implementations' stated in the class docstring is dropped. Superusers toggling the flag mid-session get cursors from one paginator interpreted by the other (offset semantics differ after the BasePaginator change), skipping or duplicating audit-log entries with no test or parity check to detect it.

[ADVISORY] The enable_advanced permission check dereferences organization_context.member without verifying member is not None — requests reaching this endpoint without an authenticated organization member (e.g. superuser accessing via a path that bypasses OrganizationAuditPermission's member resolution) hit AttributeError. A superuser with no membership row for the organization requesting optimized_pagination=true gets a 500 instead of a decision; the None-member edge case is unhandled.

[BUG] The 'performance optimization' in the shared paginator's get_result changes negative offset handling for every endpoint in the codebase, not just the audit-log endpoint named in the PR intent. Django ORM slicing with a negative start (queryset[-5:stop]) slices from the END of the ordered dataset, so any caller that ever passes a negative cursor offset gets rows from the wrong end of the result set — this is a semantic break smuggled into shared infrastructure under a PR whose stated scope is audit-log pagination.

[ADVISORY] The optimized pagination path is gated on an undocumented query parameter 'optimized_pagination=true' plus a superuser/global-access check that no requirement in the PR statement calls for. The feature is invisible and undiscoverable: no API client, docs, or UI passes the param, so the entire OptimizedCursorPaginator path is dead code in practice; the permission gate also silently restricts a 'performance' feature to admins, which is a behavior distinction not traceable to any stated requirement (perf should be privilege-independent).

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator is a near-verbatim copy of the existing paginator get_result logic (cursor handling, hits, extra/prev handling, build_cursor) rather than a targeted override, duplicating ~90 lines of subtle pagination logic. Any future fix to boundary/cursor logic in the existing paginators must be applied twice; the copy already drifts (e.g., the prev-bounds check uses len(results) == offset + limit + extra against the raw pre-trim results list, matching OffsetPaginator but diverging from DateTimePaginator semantics), so the next maintainer of pagination behavior gets two subtly different code paths to reason about.

[ADVISORY] The 'advanced feature' negative-offset branch in OptimizedCursorPaginator is unreachable dead code: no code path in this diff ever constructs a Cursor with a negative offset, and cursors.py only adds a comment. The branch exists solely to justify the risky shared-path change; it enforces no invariant and serves no user, so the entire enable_advanced_features plumbing (constructor kwarg, endpoint wiring, branch) is untraceable to any exercised requirement and can be deleted.

[ADVISORY] The cursors.py change is a comment-only edit with no behavioral counterpart — int(offset) already accepts negative values — meaning the diff claims Cursor supports a 'feature' it always had. This is scope noise that misleads reviewers into believing a semantic change accompanies it; nothing becomes deletable or safer, and the comment asserts a capability rationale ('performance optimization') that no producer of negative offsets exists to exercise.

[BUG] The 'advanced features' negative-offset path slices an unevaluated Django queryset with a negative start index, which Django's ORM does not support. Django raises "Negative indexing is not supported" (AssertionError/ValueError) when the queryset with queryset[start_offset:stop] where start_offset < 0 is evaluated, so any admin client that sends a cursor with a negative offset under optimized_pagination=true gets a 500 instead of a page of audit logs.

[BUG] The base get_result change passes a negative offset straight through for prev cursors: `start_offset = ... else offset` then `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, reintroducing the same unsupported negative slicing in the shared BasePaginator used by every endpoint. Any paginator (DateTimePaginator, OffsetPaginator, etc.) receiving a prev cursor with a negative offset — previously rejected by the ORM error path uniformly, now explicitly routed to a negative slice — crashes the request for all API consumers of BasePaginator, not just this new feature.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls int(math.floor(value)) / int(math.ceil(value)) on a datetime attribute, and value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor value with no conversion, so the paginator is used on the audit-log endpoint whose key is the `datetime` DateTimeField. int(datetime) raises TypeError when building the next cursor, and build_queryset compares a millisecond-epoch int against the datetime column producing wrong/no results — the entire optimized path is non-functional for the only endpoint wired to it.

[BUG] The prev-cursor trimming check uses `offset` (`len(results) == offset + limit + extra`) after results were sliced from `start_offset`, so when offset < 0 the comparison is off by |offset| and the last row is wrongly kept or dropped. Clients paginating backwards with a negative-offset cursor see a duplicated or missing row at the page boundary, silently corrupting the pagination stream.

[BUG] The pagination-shape switch is gated on the raw query param `optimized_pagination == "true"` with no feature flag, options entry, or org-level setting, and authorization is computed inline as `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`. The behavior cannot be disabled or rolled back without a code deploy, and for a superuser who is not a member of the org, `organization_context.member` is None and the `has_global_access` attribute access raises AttributeError, 500ing the audit-log endpoint for superusers — while the previous code path worked for them.

[ADVISORY] The two paginators emit different cursor-value semantics (DateTimePaginator encodes a datetime as ms; OptimizedCursorPaginator treats the value as a bare int), so a client that obtains a cursor under one mode and follows it under the other mode gets a mismatched comparison. Any client or script that toggles optimized_pagination between requests while reusing cursors silently pages to the wrong position or empty results; the response shape of the endpoint changes mode-to-mode behind an untyped string flag.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates ~70 lines of BasePaginator/DateTimePaginator get_result logic (cursor handling, hits, extra, trimming, build_cursor, post_query_filter) rather than subclassing DateTimePaginator, and the copies have already diverged (the prev-trim off-by bug above exists only in the copy). The next bugfix or change to pagination semantics in BasePaginator must be replicated by hand here and will drift, exactly as the offset-vs-start_offset divergence in this diff already demonstrates; deleting the duplicated body and subclassing DateTimePaginator removes the divergence risk entirely.

[ADVISORY] `Cursor(0, 0, 0)` as the None-cursor default plus `cursor_value = 0` when falsy bakes in 0 as a sentinel meaning 'start of dataset', which coincides with epoch-0 as a real datetime value, making 'no cursor' and 'cursor at epoch' indistinguishable. For any timestamped key where 0 is a representable value, the initial page and a client-constructed cursor at value 0 produce identical querysets, so the sentinel 'nothing here' is conflated with a real position — the next editor adding a value-0 test or data hits this silently.

[ADVISORY] The new paginator's docstring and inline comments ("backward compatibility", "permissions are checked at the queryset level", "Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically") describe behavior the code does not have — Django does not handle negative slicing, and permission checks are irrelevant to slicing correctness. A future maintainer relying on these comments will assume the negative-offset path is safe and supported, and will copy the pattern into other paginators, propagating the crash.

[BUG] The OptimizedCursorPaginator's enable_advanced_features path executes queryset[negative:stop], and Django ORM negative slicing raises AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported'), so any request carrying a negative cursor offset with optimized_pagination=true crashes with a 500 instead of returning results. Authenticated superusers hitting the new paginator with a negative offset get a server error, not the promised 'advanced pagination'; the comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually false.

[BUG] The review iteration silently changed the PR's stated objective from 'performance optimization of audit log pagination' into an opt-in feature branch gated on a hidden query param (optimized_pagination=true) plus an ad-hoc permission check, with no feature flag, API contract change, or explicit human acceptance of the new behavior. The shipped endpoint now has two divergent pagination code paths; the optimized path is only reachable by clients that know the undocumented param, so the performance goal is not achieved for normal traffic, and operators cannot disable the new behavior without a code deploy.

[BUG] The permission gate references organization_context.member.has_global_access (no parentheses, and organization_context is not defined in this scope), raising NameError for non-superuser requests when evaluated as part of the or expression. Every request where request.user.is_superuser is falsy crashes with NameError/AttributeError before pagination runs, returning a 500 on the previously working audit log endpoint.

[ADVISORY] The BasePaginator.get_result change alters offset semantics for all existing paginators when cursor.is_prev and offset is negative: it passes the raw negative offset into queryset[offset:stop], which Django rejects, whereas the prior code would have produced the same crash only via the (already negative) offset — the effective new behavior is that the max(0, offset) clamp is skipped for prev cursors, changing results/cursor math for every existing consumer of this base class, not just the new audit-log path. Any existing endpoint using a prev cursor with a negative offset now takes a different code path than before the diff; the base-class contract changed as a side effect of a feature scoped to audit logs, without that drift being part of the accepted intent.

[ADVISORY] The Cursor class gained only a comment claiming negative-offset support, but no validation, parsing, or serialization change — comments asserting a capability the code does not implement is intent drift embedded in the artifact. Future readers and reviewers will assume negative offsets are a supported, tested cursor feature and build on it, while the only code paths that accept them crash on the ORM slice.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result executes queryset slicing with a client-controlled negative offset (`results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` where start_offset = cursor.offset < 0), which the Django ORM does not support. Django's QuerySet slicing raises AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported') on any negative slice, so a user (any global-access member or superuser, since cursor offset is decoded from the client-supplied cursor token with no lower-bound validation in this class) who crafts a cursor with a negative offset gets an unhandled 500 instead of a 4xx — the 'safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions' comment is false.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls int(math.floor(value))/int(math.ceil(value)) on the key attribute, which is a datetime for this endpoint (order_by='-datetime'). int() on a datetime raises TypeError, so whenever this paginator is used (organization_auditlogs with optimized_pagination=true and a global-access user) and get_item_key is invoked (prev-cursor dedup in get_result and key computation in build_cursor), the request crashes with a 500.

[ADVISORY] The in-code justification 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level' asserts that auth scope alone makes client-controlled negative offsets safe, but the actual pagination-bounds contract (max_limit, MAX_HITS_LIMIT, offset clamping) is bypassed on this branch. The next maintainer reading this comment will treat negative-offset cursors as validated; any endpoint that scopes visibility via post_query_filter or on_results (not queryset-level) would leak out-of-bound rows, and even here the branch skips the max(0, offset) clamp the sibling code path enforces, producing inconsistent page contents between admin and non-admin callers of the same endpoint.

[ADVISORY] A new behavior-gated code path is switched on by the raw query parameter optimized_pagination=true with no feature flag, options entry, or rollout mechanism, and gated on an ad-hoc authorization expression (request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access) that differs from how the rest of the endpoint authorizes. Operators cannot disable the new paginator path without a code deploy, and the divergent authz expression (organization_context.member.has_global_access evaluated with a possible None member on requests where the base permission check passed via a different route) becomes a fork in the endpoint's security posture that future edits must keep in sync.

[BUG] The advanced-features branch slices the queryset with a negative start offset, which Django's ORM rejects with ValueError ('Negative indexing is not supported'), so the request crashes instead of returning a page. Any admin hitting the endpoint with optimized_pagination=true and a cursor carrying a negative offset gets an unhandled ValueError → HTTP 500; the 'negative offset pagination' feature can never return data because Django never executes queryset[-N:stop].

[BUG] The shared BasePaginator.get_result change passes cursor.offset through unclamped when cursor.is_prev is set, so a forged/malformed prev-cursor with a negative offset reaches queryset[offset:stop] and raises the same negative-index ValueError. Any client supplying a crafted cursor with is_prev=true and offset<0 (the Cursor constructor in this diff explicitly permits negative offsets via int(offset)) triggers a 500 on the previously-safe DateTimePaginator path — a regression for all existing endpoints, not just the new flag.

[BUG] Cursor now documents and accepts negative offsets as a supported 'performance optimization', institutionalizing a value the paginator layer cannot consume (Django ORM forbids negative slicing), so persisted cursors with negative offsets poison every subsequent page request. Clients that bookmark/share a cursor after a 500 or an edge-case response carry the negative offset forward, permanently breaking pagination for that session; the comment asserts a safety property ('enables efficient reverse pagination') the code does not have.

[BUG] The prev-cursor trimming logic 'elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra' compares against the raw (possibly negative) cursor.offset, so when offset<0 the comparison can never match the actual slice length, dropping the boundary-trim step and returning a duplicate row that DateTimePaginator would have removed. Administrators paginating backwards with the optimized paginator see the last item of the previous page repeated at the start of each prev page — silent data duplication rather than loss, but the pagination contract (no overlap between adjacent pages) is broken.

[ADVISORY] The optimized path reads 'organization_context.member.has_global_access' without any None/context guard and gates a new pagination contract on a raw query string flag with no feature flag, so behavior can only be toggled by code deploy and the attribute access can crash for superusers hitting the endpoint outside an organization context. A superuser with optimized_pagination=true on a request where organization_context is not populated (or member is None) gets an AttributeError → 500; operators cannot disable the new paginator path via configuration, only by rolling back the deploy.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator is ~80 lines that duplicate BasePaginator.get_result line-for-line except for the negative-offset branch, and the duplicated block has already drifted (uses cursor.offset instead of the clamped offset, recomputes slicing), so future fixes to the base paginator will not propagate to the admin path. The next maintainer who fixes a boundary bug in BasePaginator.get_result (e.g., the prev-trim logic) leaves the admin-facing copy broken; deleting the subclass and adding the flag to BasePaginator removes ~70 duplicated lines and the drift risk.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls math.floor/math.ceil on the raw field value, which for this endpoint's '-datetime' ordering is a datetime, so every optimized request returning rows crashes with TypeError before a response is built. Any admin passing optimized_pagination=true on organization audit logs gets a raw 500 instead of a 200; DateTimePaginator's version of this method converts the datetime to a timestamp (int(...timestamp(...))) before flooring — this copy dropped that conversion.

[BUG] The enable_advanced_features negative-offset path slices queryset[negative:stop], and Django querysets do not support negative slice bounds, so the ORM raises ValueError('Negative indexing is not supported') instead of 'automatically handling' it as the comment claims. The first client that sends a cursor with a negative offset to the optimized endpoint gets an unhandled ValueError surfaced as a 500, not a 4xx or a bounded page — the code path can never return results.

[BUG] In DateTimePaginator.get_result the prev-page branch leaves start_offset = cursor.offset unclamped, so a client-crafted cursor with a negative offset (cursor.offset is client-controlled base64) now takes the explicit negative-slice path and raises the Django ValueError, where the surrounding clamp logic shows the intent was to bound it. A malformed/hostile cursor on the previously working audit-log endpoint turns into an unhandled 500; before this diff the same request also sliced with a raw negative offset but the added max(0,...) clamp demonstrates the boundary was supposed to be handled and is only half-applied.

[BUG] The prev-page dedup check compares len(results) == offset + limit + extra using the unclamped offset while results were sliced from start_offset = max(0, offset), so whenever offset < 0 on a non-prev... on prev paths the length check is against the wrong arithmetic and the cursor-equality fallback silently keeps or drops the wrong row. Pages served after the clamp carry a duplicated or missing boundary row relative to what build_cursor's offset bookkeeping assumes, producing silently wrong audit-log pages (rows repeated or skipped between pages) with a 200 status.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator is a ~95-line near-verbatim copy of the existing DateTimePaginator/OffsetPaginator get_result including the duplicated get_item_key, and the two copies have already drifted (the datetime-to-int conversion is missing here), so every future paginator fix must now be applied twice. The next maintainer fixing a cursor bug in paginator.py fixes one copy and the audit-log endpoint keeps the broken twin; the drift has already produced the P1 TypeError above.

[ADVISORY] The new behavior is gated on a raw query parameter optimized_pagination=true plus an inline is_superuser/has_global_access check, with no feature flag or options entry, so it cannot be disabled or rolled back without a code deploy. If the optimized path misbehaves in production (as the TypeError finding says it will on first use), operators have no kill switch and must deploy code; also the per-request permission check organization_context.member.has_global_access will AttributeError when member is falsy, taking down the whole GET for organizations where the actor has no membership row.

[ADVISORY] cursor_value is selected with truthiness (if cursor.value:) instead of presence, so a legitimate cursor value of 0 (epoch-zero timestamp, or offset-0 value types where 0 is in-domain) is treated as absent and build_queryset runs with cursor_value=0, restarting pagination from the dataset head. A user paginating to the boundary where the key value is 0 silently gets the first page again instead of an empty continuation, with a 200 and no indication state reset.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The 'advanced features' negative-offset path passes a negative start to Django queryset slicing, which raises ValueError('Negative indexing is not supported.') Django ORM slices do not 'handle boundary conditions automatically' as the comment claims; a cursor carrying a negative offset with enable_advanced_features=True raises a 500 on every request, contradicting the docstring's promise of negative offset support — the feature's only distinct behavior is the one that crashes.

[BUG] The prev-cursor boundary handling compares len(results) against offset + limit + extra computed from the raw negative offset, mismatching the actual slice bounds start_offset + limit + extra. For a negative offset prev cursor, the elif branch never fires when it should (or fires when it shouldn't), so the duplicated boundary row is returned to the client, producing a duplicated audit-log row in the response.

adjudication.rationale: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is on and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code slices using `start_offset = cursor.offset` and `stop = start_offset + limit + extra` (`results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`). However, the subsequent prev-cursor boundary check still uses `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` where `offset` is the raw (negative) `cursor.offset`, not the effective slice window length (`stop - start_offset`). With a negative offset, `offset + limit + extra` is smaller than the actual slice size, so this condition will be wrong (often never true), meaning the intended trimming (`results = results[:-1]`) can fail and can leave an extra boundary row (potential duplication) in prev pagination.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The unconditional change to BasePaginator.get_result alters behavior for every existing paginator: when cursor.is_prev is true the offset is no longer clamped, allowing negative start_offset in the shared slice. Any existing endpoint paginating backwards with a crafted negative cursor offset now produces queryset[-N:...] which raises ValueError, turning a previously-clamped request into a 500 across all DateTimePaginator/OrganizationPaginator-style endpoints.

adjudication.rationale: The diff in `BasePaginator.get_result` does not introduce a new possibility of negative slicing for `cursor.is_prev`: it still uses `offset` directly in that branch, just as the old code did (`queryset[offset:stop]` previously). The only behavioral change is that non-`is_prev` requests now clamp `offset` to 0 via `start_offset = max(0, offset)`, which would *reduce* (not introduce) failures from negative offsets. While the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` does appear to intentionally allow negative offsets (and that may be problematic), the finding’s claim that the unconditional BasePaginator change newly turns “previously-clamped” negative offsets into 500s across endpoints is not supported by the shown diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new optimized_pagination behavior is gated on a raw query-string parameter with no settings flag or options entry, and it is the only gating flag on this path — but the sibling flag enable_advanced_features passed to paginate() is never validated to be an accepted kwarg of the paginate() signature. If Endpoint.paginate() does not forward unknown kwargs to the paginator constructor, the superuser path raises TypeError on every optimized request; operators also cannot disable the feature without a code deploy.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows the new behavior is enabled purely by a raw query parameter (`request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"`) plus an admin-style check (`request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`), with no settings/config flag to disable it at runtime. The finding’s TypeError concern hinges on how `Endpoint.paginate()` handles unknown kwargs; the diff does show an extra kwarg (`enable_advanced_features=True`) being passed to `self.paginate(...)`, but the `paginate()` signature/forwarding behavior is not shown here, so the exception claim is not directly verifiable from this diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new OptimizedCursorPaginator class (~95 lines of behavior-bearing pagination logic, including the modified shared get_result in BasePaginator) ships with no tests anywhere in the diff — no spec/test files appear, so cursor round-tripping, prev/next boundary de-duplication, and negative-offset behavior are entirely unverified. A regression in cursor construction (e.g. build_cursor consuming the mutated results list after the is_prev reverse) silently corrupts pagination for superusers browsing audit logs; nothing in the diff would catch it.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds substantial new pagination logic (new `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` ~80+ LOC) and changes shared pagination slicing behavior in `BasePaginator.get_result` (new `start_offset` computation and altered slicing). No test/spec files are added or modified anywhere in the diff to cover cursor round-tripping, `is_prev` de-duplication/reversal behavior, or the new negative-offset path (`if self.enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0: results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`). This is a concrete, diff-grounded review gap (risk of regressions) rather than a directly verifiable defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] There is no verification that OptimizedCursorPaginator returns the same rows/cursors as DateTimePaginator for the same queryset — the acceptance criterion 'backward compatibility with existing cursor implementations' stated in the class docstring is dropped. Superusers toggling the flag mid-session get cursors from one paginator interpreted by the other (offset semantics differ after the BasePaginator change), skipping or duplicating audit-log entries with no test or parity check to detect it.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a runtime switch between `DateTimePaginator` and the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` based on `optimized_pagination` (in `organization_auditlogs.py`), but nothing in the diff ensures (or even attempts to ensure) that cursors/results are compatible across the two implementations despite the new class docstring claiming “backward compatibility with existing cursor implementations.” The two code paths can apply different offset handling (BasePaginator now clamps offsets in some cases via `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`, while `OptimizedCursorPaginator` may allow negative offsets when `enable_advanced_features` is set), so using a cursor generated by one paginator with the other is a concrete, diff-grounded risk. However, the finding’s specific outcome (definite skipping/duplication in practice) is not fully verifiable from the diff alone without knowing `DateTimePaginator`’s cursor/key semantics and existing tests.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The enable_advanced permission check dereferences organization_context.member without verifying member is not None — requests reaching this endpoint without an authenticated organization member (e.g. superuser accessing via a path that bypasses OrganizationAuditPermission's member resolution) hit AttributeError. Separately, switching to `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is controlled only by a raw query param (`optimized_pagination=true`) with no feature-flag/config control shown in the diff, which is a concrete, diff-grounded operational/rollout concern rather than a proven defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator is ~80 lines that duplicate BasePaginator.get_result line-for-line except for the negative-offset branch, and the duplicated block has already drifted (uses cursor.offset instead of the clamped offset, recomputes slicing), so future fixes to the base paginator will not propagate to the admin path. The next maintainer who fixes a boundary bug in BasePaginator.get_result (e.g., the prev-trim logic) leaves the admin-facing copy broken; deleting the subclass and adding the flag to BasePaginator removes ~70 duplicated lines and the drift risk.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new ~80-line `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` that largely reimplements the existing pagination logic (cursor setup, queryset building, hit counting, offset/extra handling, prev trimming, reversing, and `build_cursor` call), with the main functional difference being the negative-offset branch gated by `enable_advanced_features`. This duplication is visible in the new class and creates a clear maintenance/drift risk. There is also already a concrete divergence in the duplicated logic: `offset = cursor.offset` is used later in the prev-trim condition `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` even though slicing may have used a clamped `start_offset` (`max(0, offset)`), so fixes/changes to the base logic (and even the new clamping change earlier in the file) won’t automatically apply to the optimized/admin path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls math.floor/math.ceil on the raw field value, which for this endpoint's '-datetime' ordering is a datetime, so every optimized request returning rows crashes with TypeError before a response is built. Any admin passing optimized_pagination=true on organization audit logs gets a raw 500 instead of a 200; DateTimePaginator's version of this method converts the datetime to a timestamp (int(...timestamp(...))) before flooring — this copy dropped that conversion.

adjudication.rationale: In `organization_auditlogs.py`, the optimized path calls `self.paginate(... paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator, order_by="-datetime" ...)`. `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key()` does `value = getattr(item, self.key)` and then applies `math.floor`/`math.ceil` to that value before `int(...)`. With `order_by="-datetime"`, `self.key` will be the `datetime` field, so `value` is a `datetime` object, and `math.floor/ceil(datetime)` will raise a `TypeError`, causing optimized requests to 500 before building a response.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The enable_advanced_features negative-offset path slices queryset[negative:stop], and Django querysets do not support negative slice bounds, so the ORM raises ValueError('Negative indexing is not supported') instead of 'automatically handling' it as the comment claims. The first client that sends a cursor with a negative offset to the optimized endpoint gets an unhandled ValueError surfaced as a 500, not a 4xx or a bounded page — the code path can never return results.

adjudication.rationale: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the `enable_advanced_features` path explicitly allows `start_offset = cursor.offset` when `cursor.offset < 0` and then does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` (negative slice start). Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing/slicing bounds and raise an exception (e.g., `ValueError('Negative indexing is not supported')`), contradicting the comment that the ORM "properly handles" it. Since the endpoint enables `enable_advanced_features=True` for the optimized paginator, a client-provided cursor with a negative offset will trigger this path and can surface as a 500 rather than returning a bounded page.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] In DateTimePaginator.get_result the prev-page branch leaves start_offset = cursor.offset unclamped, so a client-crafted cursor with a negative offset (cursor.offset is client-controlled base64) now takes the explicit negative-slice path and raises the Django ValueError, where the surrounding clamp logic shows the intent was to bound it. A malformed/hostile cursor on the previously working audit-log endpoint turns into an unhandled 500; before this diff the same request also sliced with a raw negative offset but the added max(0,...) clamp demonstrates the boundary was supposed to be handled and is only half-applied.

adjudication.rationale: In `DateTimePaginator.get_result`, the new clamp only applies when `not cursor.is_prev` (`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`). That leaves the `is_prev` path using a potentially negative `cursor.offset` directly in `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, which in Django queryset slicing can raise on negative indexes. Since `Cursor.offset` is set from client-provided cursor data (`self.offset = int(offset)` in `sentry/utils/cursors.py`), a crafted cursor can trigger an unhandled exception/500. The diff shows an intent to bound offsets (via `max(0, ...)`) but it is only half-applied.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The prev-page dedup check compares len(results) == offset + limit + extra using the unclamped offset while results were sliced from start_offset = max(0, offset), so whenever offset < 0 on a non-prev... on prev paths the length check is against the wrong arithmetic and the cursor-equality fallback silently keeps or drops the wrong row. Pages served after the clamp carry a duplicated or missing boundary row relative to what build_cursor's offset bookkeeping assumes, producing silently wrong audit-log pages (rows repeated or skipped between pages) with a 200 status.

adjudication.rationale: In the modified BasePaginator.get_result, the slice clamp (`start_offset = max(0, offset)`) only applies when `not cursor.is_prev`; the “prev-page dedup” block (`if cursor.is_prev and cursor.value: ... elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra`) only executes when `cursor.is_prev` is true, in which case `start_offset` is set to `offset` (no clamp). So the finding’s claimed mismatch between a clamped `start_offset` slice and an unclamped `offset` length check on prev paths is not supported by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator is a ~95-line near-verbatim copy of the existing DateTimePaginator/OffsetPaginator get_result including the duplicated get_item_key, and the two copies have already drifted (the datetime-to-int conversion is missing here), so every future paginator fix must now be applied twice. The next maintainer fixing a cursor bug in paginator.py fixes one copy and the audit-log endpoint keeps the broken twin; the drift has already produced the P1 TypeError above.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new ~90+ line `OptimizedCursorPaginator` in `sentry/api/paginator.py` whose `get_result` largely duplicates existing paginator logic (cursor setup, queryset build, hit counting, offset/extra handling, prev handling, reverse, `build_cursor`, post-filter), and the endpoint conditionally switches to it (`organization_auditlogs.py`). This creates a real maintainability/architecture risk: future cursor/pagination bugfixes will need to be applied in multiple places and can drift. However, the finding’s specific claim about a datetime-to-int conversion already missing here and a resulting "P1 TypeError" is not directly verifiable from the shown diff (we don't see `DateTimePaginator.get_item_key` or the referenced error), so it’s not a provable defect purely from the provided changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new behavior is gated on a raw query parameter optimized_pagination=true plus an inline is_superuser/has_global_access check, with no feature flag or options entry, so it cannot be disabled or rolled back without a code deploy. If the optimized path misbehaves in production (as the TypeError finding says it will on first use), operators have no kill switch and must deploy code; also the per-request permission check organization_context.member.has_global_access will AttributeError when member is falsy, taking down the whole GET for organizations where the actor has no membership row.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly gates the new paginator path on a raw query parameter (`use_optimized = request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"`) plus an inline permission check (`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`), with no feature-flag/setting-based kill switch shown in the change. That is a real operability/rollback concern grounded in the diff. The finding’s additional claim that `organization_context.member` can be falsy and cause an `AttributeError` is plausible from the code (no null-check), but the diff alone does not establish that `member` can be `None` in this endpoint, so that part can’t be verified here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] cursor_value is selected with truthiness (if cursor.value:) instead of presence, so a legitimate cursor value of 0 (epoch-zero timestamp, or offset-0 value types where 0 is in-domain) is treated as absent and build_queryset runs with cursor_value=0, restarting pagination from the dataset head. A user paginating to the boundary where the key value is 0 silently gets the first page again instead of an empty continuation, with a 200 and no indication state reset.

adjudication.rationale: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the truthiness check `if cursor.value:` falls back to `cursor_value = 0`, but `value_from_cursor` simply returns `cursor.value` unchanged. Therefore, for a legitimate cursor value of integer `0`, both branches produce the same `cursor_value` (0), so it does not “restart pagination from the dataset head” as claimed. While other conditionals also use `and cursor.value` (e.g., `if cursor.is_prev and cursor.value:`), the finding’s specific described behavior (silent reset to first page due to `build_queryset` running with 0) is not supported by the diff, and in this PR the paginator is used for audit log `datetime` ordering where a key of 0 is not shown to be in-domain.
